items.stem: By what percentage did sales in the South region change between 2023 and 2024?

steps: The base is the starting year (2023 = 180), not the end year.
explanation.shortcut: 9 out of 180 is 1/20: recognising simple fractions (1/20 = 5%) saves you the division.
explanation.trap: Dividing by 171 (the end year) gives -5.3%; writing the absolute change as a percentage gives -9.0%; +8.9% is the 2023-2025 comparison.
explanation.rule: % change = (New - Old) / Old × 100, with the starting year as the base.

items.stem: Which region recorded the largest percentage increase in sales between 2024 and 2025?

steps: The highest percentage growth is South (14.6%).
explanation.shortcut: Compare the absolute increases first (26, 25, 7, 22): North and South are similar, but South starts from a much smaller base (171 versus 264), so it grows more in percentage terms.
explanation.trap: Choosing North because it has the largest absolute increase (+26). The question asks for the percentage change.
explanation.rule: For the same absolute increase, the smaller base wins in percentage terms.

items.stem: If North sales grow in 2026 at the same percentage rate as in 2025 and all other regions stay at their 2025 levels, what share of total 2026 sales will North represent (to the nearest 0.1%)?

explanation.shortcut: Round the growth to about +10%: North ≈ 319, total ≈ 932, share ≈ 34%. Among the options only 34.2% fits.
explanation.trap: Dividing 318.6 by the 2025 total (903) gives 35.3%: the denominator must also include North's growth. Using the 2023-2025 growth (+20.8%) leads to 36.4%; 32.1% is the 2025 share; dividing by the other regions only (318.6 / 613) gives 52.0%.
explanation.rule: When you project one component, recalculate the total as well before computing the share.

items.stem: By what percentage did Subscriptions revenue increase from Q1 to Q4 2025?

explanation.trap: Dividing by 73 (the final value) gives 17.8%; reading the wrong series gives 14.3% (Services) or 31.0% (Licences); 13.0% mistakes the absolute increase for a percentage.
explanation.rule: In a bar chart, check the series and the period before calculating; the base is the starting period.

items.stem: What percentage of full-year 2025 revenue came from Services (to the nearest 0.1%)?

explanation.shortcut: One fifth of 563 is 112.6: 117 is slightly above that, so the share is slightly above 20%.
explanation.trap: Using a single quarter: Q4 gives 32 / 160 = 20.0%, Q1 gives 28 / 130 = 21.5%. Dividing by the other lines (117 / 446) gives 26.2%; 33.3% assumes three lines of equal weight.
explanation.rule: Share = part / overall total for the same period, summing all the quarters.

items.stem: Assume Licences revenue grows by 10% every quarter in 2026, starting from the Q4 2025 level (so Q1 2026 = Q4 2025 × 1.10). What would total Licences revenue be for 2026 (to the nearest USD m)?

explanation.trap: Using 55 as the first quarter (55 + 60.5 + 66.55 + 73.21 = 255), applying 10% to the 2025 total (180 × 1.1 = 198) or multiplying Q1 2026 by 4 (242); 55 × 4 = 220 ignores growth altogether.
explanation.rule: With compound growth per period, each term grows on the previous one: add up the individual terms.

items.stem: What was the price per unit in the United States expressed in euros?

steps: US price: USD 56.70. Exchange rate: 1 EUR = 1.08 USD.
To go from USD to EUR, divide by the exchange rate: 56.70 / 1.08 = 52.50.
explanation.trap: Multiplying by 1.08 (61.24) or deducting 8% (56.70 × 0.92 = 52.16): dividing by 1.08 is not the same as subtracting 8%. 48.76 multiplies by the sterling rate (56.70 × 0.86), i.e. it uses the wrong line of the note.
explanation.rule: If 1 EUR = X units of currency, then amount in EUR = amount in currency / X.

items.stem: What percentage of total 2025 revenue, measured in euros, came from Japan (to the nearest 0.1%)?

explanation.shortcut: Convert only the prices (the divisions give round numbers: 52.5, 50, 48), then multiply by the units.
explanation.trap: Using shares of units sold (60 / 410 = 14.6%) ignores prices; forgetting to convert the US price leads to 13.9%; 16.7% divides by the other markets instead of by the total.
explanation.rule: For a multi-currency revenue share, bring everything into the same currency before adding up.

items.stem: If the euro strengthens to 1 EUR = 1.188 USD (a 10% rise in the EUR/USD rate) and the US price and volume are unchanged, by how much would US revenue fall when measured in euros (to the nearest EUR 000)?

steps: At the current exchange rate: 8,505 / 1.08 = EUR 7,875k.
At the new exchange rate: 8,505 / 1.188 = EUR 7,159k.
explanation.shortcut: If the exchange rate rises by 10%, the euro equivalent is multiplied by 1 / 1.1 = 0.909: a fall of 9.09%. 7,875 × 0.0909 = 716.
explanation.trap: Thinking that a euro 10% stronger cuts revenue by 10% (788k): the fall is 1 - 1/1.1 = 9.1%. Taking 10% of dollar revenue (851k) or multiplying 8,505 by the change in the exchange rate (8,505 × 0.108 = 919k) mixes currencies; 7,159k is the new level, not the fall.
explanation.rule: A rise of x% in the exchange rate reduces the converted value by x / (1 + x), not by x.

items.stem: By what percentage did the German electricity price fall from Q1 to Q2 2025?

explanation.shortcut: 24 is a quarter of 96: -25%.
explanation.trap: Dividing by 72 (-33.3%) uses the wrong base; -24.0% mistakes the absolute change for a percentage; -18.8% is Italy.
explanation.rule: % reduction = (Old - New) / Old.

items.stem: A factory consumes 2,500 MWh of electricity in every quarter of 2025 and pays the average wholesale price. How much more would it have paid over the year in Italy than in Spain?

steps: Sum of quarterly prices: Italy 128 + 104 + 112 + 120 = 464; Spain 80 + 48 + 64 + 76 = 268.
Difference summed over the 4 quarters: 464 - 268 = 196 EUR/MWh.
explanation.shortcut: Average annual difference (116 - 67 = 49) × annual consumption (10,000 MWh) = 490,000.
explanation.trap: Using the difference for a single quarter (Q4: 44 × 10,000 = 440,000; Q1: 48 × 10,000 = 480,000) or a single quarter's consumption (49 × 2,500 = 122,500); 196 × 10,000 = 1,960,000 counts consumption twice.
explanation.rule: Cost = price × quantity for each period, then sum; with constant consumption, average difference × total consumption is enough.

items.stem: A buyer purchases all its electricity in France. It consumed 3,000 MWh in Q1, 2,000 MWh in Q2, 2,000 MWh in Q3 and 3,000 MWh in Q4. What was its volume-weighted average price for 2025 (EUR/MWh)?

explanation.trap: The simple average (88 + 60 + 70 + 82) / 4 = 75.0 ignores that consumption is higher in the expensive quarters; swapping the volumes (2,000 MWh in Q1 and Q4, 3,000 in Q2 and Q3) gives 73.0; 85.0 is the average of the peak quarters only.
explanation.rule: Weighted average = Σ(price × quantity) / Σ quantity.

items.stem: How many more units did Kestrel Systems ship than Halden Tech in 2025?

explanation.shortcut: Subtract the shares first, then multiply only once: 0.14 × 240,000 = 33,600.
explanation.trap: Reading the units of a single vendor (Halden 43,200; Kestrel 76,800), adding the shares (50% = 120,000) or also multiplying by the 1.2 growth (40,320).
explanation.rule: Difference in value = difference in share × total, if the total is the same.

items.stem: Orion Compute shipped 50,400 units in 2024. By what percentage did its unit shipments change in 2025?

explanation.trap: Dividing by 57,600 gives 12.5%; using market growth (20%) ignores the share; -4.8% is the change in share (from 25.2% to 24%), not in units, and 24.0% is the share itself.
explanation.rule: Volume = share × market: the share can fall while units rise, if the market grows enough.

items.stem: If the total market grows by a further 15% in 2026 and Kestrel's market share falls by 4 percentage points, how many units will Kestrel ship in 2026 (to the nearest 100)?

explanation.trap: Reading '4 percentage points' as a relative -4% (32% × 0.96 = 30.72%, i.e. 84,800), forgetting market growth (67,200) or leaving the share unchanged (88,300). Making the first two mistakes together (76,800 × 0.96) gives 73,700.
explanation.rule: Percentage points are subtracted from the share; relative percentages multiply it.

items.stem: By what percentage did Technology headcount increase from 2024 to 2025 (to the nearest 0.1%)?

explanation.shortcut: 75 / 380 is just below 76 / 380 = 20%: hence 19.7%.
explanation.trap: Dividing by 455 gives 16.5%; 14.3% is Technology's share of 2025 headcount, not its growth; 7.1% and 12.1% are Corporate banking and Risk & compliance.
explanation.rule: % growth = increase / starting value.

items.stem: What was the average salary across all five departments in 2025, weighted by headcount (to the nearest EUR 100)?

explanation.shortcut: Retail (37% of employees) has a salary of 48 and Operations 41: the average must sit below the simple average of 58.8. That leaves only 53-54k, and the calculation decides between them.
explanation.trap: The simple average of salaries (294 / 5 = 58.8) ignores the weights; dividing by 2024 headcount (3,200) gives 54,000; weighting by 2024 headcount gives 53,100; 65,000 is the median salary.
explanation.rule: Weighted average = Σ(weight × value) / Σ weights, with weights and values from the same year.

items.stem: In 2026 the bank plans to cut Operations headcount by 15% from its 2025 level and to hire the same number of people into Technology. What would Technology headcount be in 2026?

explanation.trap: Applying 15% to Technology (455 × 1.15 = 523), using Operations 2024 (860 × 15% = 129, so 584) or answering with the new Operations headcount (780 - 117 = 663).
explanation.rule: Check which base the percentage applies to and which row the result goes to.

items.stem: By what percentage did actual Digital spend exceed the Digital budget in 2025?

explanation.trap: Dividing by actual (120 / 920 = 13.0%); comparing with 2024 actual (920 / 700 = +31.4%); 16.0% is the Events column; 3.9% is the total variance.
explanation.rule: Variance vs budget = (Actual - Budget) / Budget.

items.stem: Across all four channels, what was the variance of total actual 2025 spend against the total 2025 budget?

explanation.shortcut: 70 / 1,800 = 7 / 180 ≈ 3.9%; over budget because actual exceeds budget.
explanation.trap: Dividing by actual (70 / 1,870 = 3.7%), comparing with the previous year (1,870 / 1,780 = +5.1%) or adding only the overruns (120 + 40 = 160 out of 1,800, i.e. 8.9%) while ignoring the savings on TV and Print. Watch the sign: spending more than budget is an overspend.
explanation.rule: Add up the rows first, then calculate the variance against the total budget.

items.stem: For 2026, each channel's budget is set at its 2025 actual spend plus 5%, except Print, whose budget is cut to 50% of its 2025 actual spend. What share of the 2026 total budget will Digital represent (to the nearest 0.1%)?

explanation.shortcut: The +5% rows can be calculated as a block: (1,870 - 120) × 1.05 + 60 = 1,837.5 + 60 = 1,897.5.
explanation.trap: Cutting Print by 50% from budget instead of from actual (75 instead of 60) gives 50.5%; 49.2% is the 2025 actual share and 44.4% the 2025 budget share (800 / 1,800); dropping Print entirely gives 52.6%.
explanation.rule: Recalculate each component with its own rule, then the total, then the share.

items.stem: What is the NPL ratio (non-performing loans as a percentage of gross loans) for the Real estate sector?

steps: Real estate: NPL = 288, gross loans = 3,200 (EUR m).
explanation.trap: 288 / 770 = 37.4% is Real estate's share of total NPLs, not its NPL ratio; 5.9% is the ratio for the whole bank; 7.0% is Retail.
explanation.rule: NPL ratio = NPL / gross loans of the same sector.

items.stem: Which sector has the highest provision coverage ratio (provisions as a percentage of non-performing loans)?

steps: The highest is Energy (60.4%), just above Real estate (60.1%).
explanation.shortcut: Discard the 50% and 55% ratios, then use 60% as a threshold: 0.6 × 288 = 172.8 and 0.6 × 48 = 28.8. Both exceed it by 0.2, but 0.2 out of 48 weighs far more than 0.2 out of 288.
explanation.trap: Choosing Real estate because it has the highest absolute provisions (173) or because it looks like 'about 60%' just as Energy does, without checking the decimal.
explanation.rule: When two ratios are close, compare each one's excess over a common threshold in proportion to its base.

items.stem: The bank sells EUR 200m of Real estate non-performing loans. Assuming nothing else changes, what would the bank's total NPL ratio be after the sale (to the nearest 0.1%)?

steps: NPLs are included in gross loans, so the sale reduces both: NPL 770 - 200 = 570; gross loans 13,000 - 200 = 12,800.
explanation.shortcut: Remove the same amount from numerator and denominator: 570 / 12,800 ≈ 4.45%.
explanation.trap: Leaving the denominator unchanged (570 / 13,000 = 4.4%) forgets that the loans sold also leave gross loans; 2.9% is the new ratio for Real estate alone (88 / 3,000).
explanation.rule: If an item is included in the total, when you remove it from the numerator remove it from the denominator too.

items.stem: What were the total net flows across the three funds in Q2 2025?

explanation.shortcut: Add the positives (100) and subtract the negatives (40): 60.
explanation.trap: Ignoring the sign of the Equity outflow (40 + 90 + 10 = 140), excluding it altogether (90 + 10 = 100) or reading another quarter (Q1 = 160, Q3 = 230).
explanation.rule: Negative net flows are subtracted: always check the sign below zero.

items.stem: Ignoring market movements, by what percentage did the Fixed income fund's AUM increase during 2025 as a result of net flows (to the nearest 0.1%)?

explanation.trap: Ignoring the Q4 outflow (260 / 1,800 = 14.4%) or adding it as a positive (290 / 1,800 = 16.1%); dividing by closing AUM (230 / 2,030) gives 11.3%; 9.6% uses Equity's AUM.
explanation.rule: Growth from flows = net flows for the year / AUM at the start of the year.

items.stem: Which fund received the highest full-year net flows relative to its AUM at 1 January 2025?

steps: Annual flows: Equity 120 - 40 + 80 + 150 = 310; Fixed income 60 + 90 + 110 - 30 = 230; Multi-asset -20 + 10 + 40 + 70 = 100.
Ratio to opening AUM: Equity 310 / 2,400 = 12.9%; Fixed income 230 / 1,800 = 12.8%; Multi-asset 100 / 800 = 12.5%.
The highest is Equity, if only narrowly.
explanation.shortcut: Use 12.5% (= 1/8) as a threshold: Equity 2,400 / 8 = 300 (excess of 10 on 2,400), Fixed income 225 (excess of 5 on 1,800), Multi-asset exactly 100. Equity wins.
explanation.trap: Choosing Multi-asset because it has the strongest quarterly trend in the chart, or 'All three are equal' because the ratios all look to be around 12-13%.
explanation.rule: For relative comparisons, use a common threshold and measure how far each one exceeds it.

items.stem: Which route generates the highest ticket revenue per flight?

steps: Revenue per flight = seats × load factor × fare (the number of flights is not needed).
explanation.shortcut: Ignore weekly flights and compare passengers per flight × fare: the candidates are Milan-London (153 × 120) and Rome-Berlin (135 × 130).
explanation.trap: Choosing Naples-Munich because it has the highest fare (140) while ignoring its low load factor, or weighting by the number of flights when the question asks for revenue per flight.
explanation.rule: Revenue per unit = volume per unit × price: eliminate the irrelevant factors before calculating.

items.stem: How many empty seats per week are there on the Milan-Madrid and Rome-Berlin routes combined?

explanation.shortcut: Empty seats = seats × (1 - load factor), row by row, then sum.
explanation.trap: Applying the average load factor (17.5% empty on average) to total seats (4,620) gives about 809, but the routes have different capacities; 3,780 is the number of passengers; 210 is Rome-Berlin only.
explanation.rule: Do not average percentages with different bases: calculate the quantities row by row.

items.stem: Skyline plans to increase Naples-Munich to 14 flights per week. It expects the route's load factor to fall to 60% and the average fare to fall by 10%. By how much would weekly ticket revenue on the route increase?

explanation.trap: Forgetting the fall in the fare (+73,500) or in the load factor (+82,320); simply doubling revenue (+102,900); 158,760 is the new revenue, not the increase.
explanation.rule: Revenue = flights × seats × load factor × fare: update each factor and compare with the starting level.

items.stem: What was the gross profit of Power modules in 2025?

steps: Power modules revenue 2025: EUR 220m (from the note).
explanation.trap: Using the 2024 margin (33%, so 72.6) or the Connectors margin (30%, 66.0); 151.8 is the cost of goods sold (69%); 6.8 is a scale error.
explanation.rule: Gross profit = revenue × gross margin for the same line and the same year.

items.stem: What was the overall gross margin across the four product lines in 2025 (to the nearest 0.1%)?

steps: Gross profit 2025: Sensors 150 × 47% = 70.5; Power modules 220 × 31% = 68.2; Connectors 180 × 30% = 54.0; Displays 50 × 27% = 13.5.
explanation.shortcut: Start from 30% of 600 = 180 and add the deviations: Sensors +17 points × 150 = 25.5; Power +1 × 220 = 2.2; Displays -3 × 50 = -1.5. Total 206.2.
explanation.trap: The simple average of the margins (135 / 4 = 33.8%) ignores the revenue weights; using the 2024 margins gives 34.2%; excluding Displays gives 35.0%; 30.5% is the median.
explanation.rule: The aggregate margin is the revenue-weighted average of the margins.

items.stem: In 2026 Sensors revenue is expected to grow by 20%, and its gross margin to improve by the same number of percentage points as between 2024 and 2025. By how much would Sensors gross profit increase from 2025 to 2026?

explanation.shortcut: Round numbers: 180 × 0.5 = 90; then subtract 70.5.
explanation.trap: Holding the margin flat (180 × 47% = 84.6, so +14.1), using the 2023-2025 change (+5 points, so +23.1) or forgetting revenue growth (+4.5); 90.0 is the 2026 level, not the increase.
explanation.rule: Change in profit = new (revenue × margin) - old (revenue × margin): update both factors.

items.stem: What was export revenue to the United Kingdom in 2024, measured in euros?

steps: UK 2024: GBP 21.5m. 2024 exchange rate: 1 EUR = 0.86 GBP.
explanation.shortcut: Check: 25 × 0.86 = 21.5. With an exchange rate below 1, the euro value must be higher than the sterling value.
explanation.trap: Multiplying by 0.86 (18.5) or not converting (21.5); 23.7 is the 2025 figure in sterling; 20.0 is Switzerland.
explanation.rule: Amount in EUR = amount in currency / (units of currency per 1 EUR).

items.stem: Measured in euros, by what percentage did export revenue to the United States grow from 2024 to 2025 (to the nearest 0.1%)?

explanation.shortcut: Growth in euros = (1 + local growth) × (old rate / new rate) - 1 = 1.20 × 1.08 / 1.12 - 1 = 15.7%.
explanation.trap: Growth in dollars (20.0%) ignores the exchange rate; subtracting the FX move (20% - 3.7% = 16.3%) is only an approximation; multiplying by the exchange rate instead of dividing gives 24.4%.
explanation.rule: Convert each year at its own exchange rate, then calculate growth: the effects multiply, they do not add.

items.stem: In 2026 export revenue to Japan is expected to grow by 10% in yen, and the exchange rate to move to 1 EUR = 160 JPY. What would Japanese export revenue be in euros (to the nearest EUR 0.1m)?

explanation.shortcut: Work in millions of yen to avoid scale errors: 2,970 / 160 = 297 / 16 = 18.56.
explanation.trap: Using the 2025 exchange rate (2,970 / 168 = 17.7), forgetting growth (2,700 / 160 = 16.9), starting from 2024 (2,400 × 1.1 / 160 = 16.5) or keeping the 2025 value (2,700 / 168 = 16.1).
explanation.rule: First project in local currency, then convert at the exchange rate for the projected period.

items.stem: What was Industrial segment revenue in 2025?

explanation.trap: 0.42bn is Industrial's EBITDA (1.92 × 22%), not its revenue; 0.96 and 1.20 are other slices (Consumer and Healthcare); 0.40 confuses the share with an amount.
explanation.rule: Value of a slice = % share × total given in the note.

items.stem: Which segment generated the lowest EBITDA in 2025?

steps: EBITDA = revenue × margin. Revenue: Consumer 20% × 4.8 = 0.96bn; Digital 15% × 4.8 = 0.72bn.
Industrial (1.92 × 22% = 422.4m) and Healthcare (1.20 × 25% = 300m) are much higher.
explanation.shortcut: Compare share × margin without using the total: Consumer 20 × 12 = 240, Digital 15 × 15 = 225. Digital is lower.
explanation.trap: Choosing Consumer because it has the lowest margin (12%): however, its revenue is higher than Digital's.
explanation.rule: Profit = size × margin: do not judge on just one of the two factors.

items.stem: Group revenue is forecast to grow by 10% in 2026, and Digital revenue by 40%. What growth rate does this imply for the other three segments combined (to the nearest 0.1%)?

explanation.shortcut: Think in terms of contributions: the group grows by 10 points; Digital weighs 15% and grows by 40%, so it contributes 6 points. That leaves 4 points, to be divided by the weight of the others (85%): 4 / 0.85 = 4.7%.
explanation.trap: Stopping at 4.0% forgets to divide by the weight of the other segments; 6.0% is Digital's contribution; 0.0% comes from forcing the simple average of the four rates to be 10% ((40 + 3x) / 4 = 10), ignoring the weights.
explanation.rule: Total growth = Σ(weight × growth): to back out a missing rate, isolate its contribution and divide by its weight.

items.stem: Which cost line had the largest overspend against budget in 2025, in absolute terms?

steps: Variance = actual - budget: Staff +625; Fuel -640; Maintenance +280; Rent 0; IT +210 (EUR 000).
Overspend means a positive variance: the largest is Staff (+625).
explanation.shortcut: Discard the rows where actual is below budget (Fuel) and compare only the positive differences.
explanation.trap: Choosing Fuel because it has the largest absolute variance (640), but it is a saving; choosing IT because it has the highest percentage overspend (15%).
explanation.rule: Check the sign and the metric required: absolute or percentage, overspend or underspend.

items.stem: If Fuel costs had come in exactly on budget, by what percentage would total actual operating costs for 2025 have exceeded the total budget (to the nearest 0.1%)?

steps: With Fuel on budget, actual rises by 640: 25,475 + 640 = 26,115.
explanation.shortcut: Add only the overspends: 625 + 280 + 210 = 1,115 out of 25,000 = 4.46%.
explanation.trap: Subtracting the Fuel saving instead of setting it to zero gives -0.7%; dividing by 26,115 gives 4.3%; 1.9% is the actual variance including Fuel; 2.6% (640 / 25,000) measures only the Fuel adjustment.
explanation.rule: 'If X were on budget' means setting X's variance to zero, not reversing it.

items.stem: For 2026, staff costs are budgeted 4% above 2025 actual, fuel 8% above 2025 actual, and every other line equal to its 2025 actual. By what percentage will the 2026 total budget exceed the 2025 total budget (to the nearest 0.1%)?

explanation.shortcut: Start from 2025 actual (25,475) and add the increases: 525 (staff) + 460.8 (fuel) = 985.8. Total 26,460.8.
explanation.trap: Comparing with 2025 actual instead of the 2025 budget gives 3.9%; applying the growth rates to the 2025 budget gives 4.0%; 2.4% is the simple average (4% + 8%) / 5; 1.9% is the 2025 variance.
explanation.rule: Distinguish the base you apply the growth to from the comparison the question asks for: they are often different.

items.stem: A household has a EUR 240,000 interest-only variable-rate mortgage charged at the average variable-rate mortgage rate for each year. How much lower was its annual interest bill in 2025 than in 2023?

explanation.trap: Using the fall in the policy rate (2.0 points, 4,800), in the fixed rate (1.1 points, 2,640) or the 2024-2025 period (1.6 points, 3,840); 504 is a scale error.
explanation.rule: Change in interest = change in rate in points × principal.

items.stem: By what percentage did the household deposit rate change from 2023 to 2025?

steps: In percentage points the change is -0.8, but the question asks for the percentage change.
explanation.shortcut: 0.8 is half of 1.6: -50%.
explanation.trap: Confusing percentage points (-0.8) with percentage change; -42.9% uses 2024 as the base; +100% inverts the ratio (1.6 / 0.8); +300% is the 2022-2025 comparison.
explanation.rule: For a rate, '% change' is relative (new / old - 1); 'change in points' is the simple difference.

items.stem: In 2025, 70% of new mortgages by value were fixed-rate and 30% were variable-rate. What was the average interest rate on new mortgages in 2025?

explanation.shortcut: Start from 3.0% and add 70% of the difference (0.3 points): 3.0 + 0.21 = 3.21%.
explanation.trap: Inverting the weights (3.09%), taking the simple average (3.15%), stopping at the first product (2.31%) or using only the fixed rate (3.30%).
explanation.rule: Weighted average of two values = lower value + weight of the higher value × difference.

items.stem: By what percentage did APAC headcount grow between 2024 and 2025?

explanation.shortcut: 180 is one fifth of 900: 20%.
explanation.trap: Dividing by 1,080 gives 16.7%; 10.6% is the growth of the whole company; 9.5% and 7.1% are Americas and EMEA.
explanation.rule: % growth = increase / starting value of the same series.

items.stem: What was the firm's overall revenue per employee in 2025 (to the nearest EUR 000)?

explanation.shortcut: Deviations from 210 (EMEA): Americas +35 × 1,610 = +56,350; APAC -30 × 1,080 = -32,400; net +23,950 / 4,870 ≈ +4.9. Result about 215.
explanation.trap: The simple average (210 + 245 + 180) / 3 = 212 ignores that EMEA and Americas have many more employees than APAC.
explanation.rule: For an aggregate ratio, add up the numerators and the denominators: never take the simple average of the ratios.

items.stem: Assume that after 2025, APAC and Americas headcount each keep growing every year at the same percentage rate as between 2024 and 2025. In which year will APAC headcount first exceed Americas headcount?

steps: In 2029 APAC (2,239) is still below Americas (2,317); in 2030 it overtakes it (2,687 vs 2,537).
explanation.shortcut: Gap to close: 1,610 / 1,080 = 1.49. Each year APAC gains 1.20 / 1.095 ≈ 1.096: after 4 years 1.44 (not enough), after 5 years 1.58 (enough). So 2030.
explanation.trap: Holding Americas flat at 1,610 leads to 2028 (APAC 1,866): the competitor is growing too.
explanation.rule: To find when one series overtakes another under compound growth, compare the initial gap with the ratio of the growth factors raised to the number of years.

items.stem: What was the Global Bond fund's AUM at the end of 2025?

explanation.trap: Applying the return before the flows (2,000 × 1.03 - 200 = 1,860), forgetting the return (1,800), forgetting the flows (2,060) or treating the outflow as an inflow (2,200 × 1.03 = 2,266).
explanation.rule: Follow the order given in the note: flows first, then the return on the new balance.

items.stem: Which fund generated the highest management fee revenue in 2025?

steps: Fees (EUR m): Equity 1,458 × 0.90% = 13.1; Bond 1,854 × 0.45% = 8.3; Infrastructure 792 × 1.20% = 9.5; Private Credit 513.6 × 1.50% = 7.7.
explanation.shortcut: Bond has about 1.27 times Equity's AUM but half the fee: it loses. Infrastructure and Private Credit have AUM too small to offset their higher fees.
explanation.trap: Choosing Global Bond (largest AUM) or Private Credit (highest fee): what matters is the product of the two factors.
explanation.rule: Fee revenue = AUM × fee rate: compare the product, not the individual factors.

items.stem: What was the AUM-weighted average management fee across the four funds, based on year-end AUM (to the nearest basis point)?

explanation.shortcut: If you already have the fees by fund, two sums and one division are enough: 38.7 / 4,618 ≈ 0.84%.
explanation.trap: Dividing the fees by opening AUM (4,200) gives 92 bp; weighting the fees by opening AUM gives 79 bp; the simple average of the fees gives 101 bp; 105 bp is the median.
explanation.rule: Weighted average fee = total fees / total AUM, on the same basis used to calculate the fees.

items.stem: By what percentage did the carbon allowance price change from 2024 to 2025 (to the nearest 0.1%)?

explanation.shortcut: 16% of 62 is 9.92, almost exactly 10: the answer is just above 16%.
explanation.trap: Dividing by 72 gives +13.9%; +10.0% confuses euros with a percentage; -14.3% is the 2023-2025 comparison; -16.1% is a sign error.
explanation.rule: Always calculate % change on the starting year given.

items.stem: Measured in euros, by what percentage did the Brent crude price fall from 2024 to 2025?

explanation.shortcut: Convert both years: the numbers become round (75 and 60), then 15 / 75 = 1/5.
explanation.trap: 16.7% is the fall in dollars; 20.8% adds the dollar fall and the FX effect (an incorrect approximation); 25.0% uses 2025 as the base; 4.2% is only the FX move.
explanation.rule: To compare prices in another currency, convert each year at its own exchange rate.

items.stem: In 2025 a utility burns 50,000 tonnes of coal and must buy 2.5 tonnes of CO2 allowances for every tonne of coal burned. At average 2025 prices, what was its combined cost of coal and carbon allowances in euros?

steps: Coal: USD 99 / 1.125 = EUR 88 per tonne; 50,000 × 88 = EUR 4.40m.
explanation.shortcut: The allowances are already in euros: convert only the coal.
explanation.trap: Not converting the coal (4.95 + 9.00 = 13.95), multiplying by the exchange rate (14.57), forgetting the 2.5 factor (8.00) or using 2024 prices (13.00).
explanation.rule: Before adding up costs, bring every item into the same currency and the same physical unit.

items.stem: How many units did Bluefin ship in 2025?

explanation.trap: Using the 2024 market (27% × 144 = 38.9m), Bluefin's 2024 figure (25% × 144 = 36.0m) or the Aster series (46.4m); 27.0m reads the share as if it were units.
explanation.rule: Units = share for the year × market for the same year.

items.stem: By what percentage did Aster's unit shipments change from 2024 to 2025 (to the nearest 0.1%)?

explanation.trap: Looking only at the share (-6.5% or -2 points) and concluding that units fell; dividing by 46.40 gives +3.8%; +11.1% is market growth.
explanation.rule: Volume = share × market: the change in volume combines the two changes by multiplying them.

items.stem: Assume the total market grows by 5% in 2026 and Corla's unit shipments grow at the same percentage rate as between 2024 and 2025. What would Corla's market share be in 2026 (to the nearest 0.1%)?

explanation.shortcut: New share = old share × (Corla growth / market growth) = 21% × 1.228 / 1.05 = 24.6%.
explanation.trap: Applying the growth to the share instead of the units (21 × 21 / 19 = 23.2%), forgetting market growth (41.26 / 160 = 25.8%) or multiplying the share by 1.05 (22.1%).
explanation.rule: Future share = current share × (1 + company growth) / (1 + market growth).

items.stem: What was the total value of non-performing loans in the retail portfolio at the end of 2025?

steps: NPLs by product = 2025 balance × NPL ratio: Mortgages 8,400 × 2% = 168.0; Consumer loans 1,800 × 6% = 108.0.
explanation.trap: Applying the simple average of the ratios (5.25%) to the total balance of 12,000 gives 630; using the 2024 balances gives 335; 168 is only the Mortgages line; 3,755 is a scale error.
explanation.rule: Total NPLs = Σ(balance × ratio) line by line, never simple average ratio × total.

items.stem: What was the balance-weighted average interest rate on the retail portfolio in 2025 (to the nearest 0.01%)?

steps: Annual interest (EUR m): Mortgages 8,400 × 3.5% = 294; Consumer 1,800 × 8.5% = 153; Credit cards 550 × 16% = 88; Auto 1,250 × 6% = 75.
explanation.shortcut: Mortgages make up 70% of the portfolio: the average rate must be much closer to 3.5% than to 16%. Rule out 7.25% and 8.50% straight away.
explanation.trap: The simple average (34 / 4 = 8.50%) ignores the weights; using the 2024 balances gives 4.98%; 7.25% is the median; 3.50% is only the mortgage rate.
explanation.rule: Portfolio average rate = total interest / total balance.

items.stem: In 2026, credit card balances are expected to grow by 20% and all other balances by 5%, with each product's NPL ratio unchanged. What would the portfolio NPL ratio be in 2026 (to the nearest 0.01%)?

explanation.shortcut: Everything grows by 5% except the extra growth in cards: NPLs = 375.5 × 1.05 + 82.5 × 9% = 394.3 + 7.4 = 401.7; balance = 12,000 × 1.05 + 82.5 = 12,682.5.
explanation.trap: Dividing the new NPLs by the old balance (401.7 / 12,000 = 3.35%), leaving the extra growth in cards out of the denominator (401.7 / 12,600 = 3.19%) or keeping the 2025 ratio unchanged (3.13%); 5.25% is the simple average of the ratios.
explanation.rule: Mix matters: if the riskiest product grows faster, the aggregate ratio rises even when the product ratios are unchanged.

items.stem: By what percentage did the Shanghai-Rotterdam rate fall from Q2 to Q4 2025 (to the nearest 0.1%)?

explanation.trap: Dividing by 2,800 gives 71.4%; 58.3% is the ratio 2,800 / 4,800 (what remains, not what is lost); 30.0% is only the Q3-Q4 fall; 12.5% is the Q1-Q4 comparison.
explanation.rule: % fall = (Old - New) / Old; the ratio New / Old shows what remains.

items.stem: A shipper sends 40 containers from Shanghai to Rotterdam in every quarter of 2025, paying the spot rate. What was its total freight cost for the year in euros (to the nearest EUR 100)?

steps: Sum of the quarterly freight rates: 3,200 + 4,800 + 4,000 + 2,800 = USD 14,800 per container per year.
explanation.shortcut: Dividing by 1.1 is the same as taking off about 9.1%: 592,000 - 53,818 = 538,182.
explanation.trap: Leaving the figure in dollars (592,000), multiplying by 1.1 (651,200) or subtracting 10% (532,800); 134,500 counts only one quarter at the average rate.
explanation.rule: Annual cost = Σ(quarterly price × quantity), then a single conversion at the end.

items.stem: A forwarder could have fixed the Shanghai-Los Angeles rate at USD 3,100 per container for all of 2025 instead of paying the spot rate each quarter. It ships 25 containers per quarter. Compared with paying spot, what would fixing the rate have meant over the year?

steps: Shanghai-Los Angeles spot: 2,600 + 4,200 + 3,600 + 2,400 = USD 12,800 per container per year (average 3,200).
explanation.shortcut: Average spot 3,200 vs fixed 3,100: a saving of 100 per container × 100 containers = 10,000.
explanation.trap: Counting only one quarter of volume (2,500), looking only at the Q2 peak (27,500) or reversing the sign (a loss).
explanation.rule: With constant volumes, compare the fixed price with the average of the spot prices and multiply by total volume.

items.stem: What was Brivio's online revenue in Q4 2025?

explanation.trap: Using another quarter's conversion rate (3.0%: 33.8m; 2.5%: 28.1m) or getting the scale of the millions wrong (3.6m); 24.0m is Q1.
explanation.rule: Revenue = visits × conversion rate × average order value, all from the same quarter.

items.stem: What was the average order value across the whole of 2025 (to the nearest cent)?

explanation.shortcut: Q4 has many more orders and the lowest AOV: the average must be below the simple average (82.50). Between 81.32 and 81.45, the calculation weighted by orders decides.
explanation.trap: The simple average of the AOVs (82.50) ignores volumes; weighting by visits instead of orders gives 81.45.
explanation.rule: An average order value must be weighted by the number of orders, not by visits or by quarters.

items.stem: For Q4 2026, Brivio expects website visits to be 10% lower and the average order value to be 4% lower than in Q4 2025. What conversion rate would be needed to keep Q4 revenue unchanged (to the nearest 0.01%)?

steps: Revenue = visits × conversion rate × AOV. Visits and AOV are multiplied by 0.90 × 0.96 = 0.864.
To hold revenue steady, the conversion rate must rise by a factor of 1 / 0.864.
explanation.shortcut: Check: 13.5m visits × 3.7037% = 500,000 orders × EUR 72 = 36.0m, unchanged.
explanation.trap: Adding the falls (10% + 4% = 14%) and computing 3.2% × 1.14 = 3.65% underestimates what is needed; offsetting only one factor gives 3.33% or 3.56%.
explanation.rule: In a product of factors, to offset a fall you divide by the product of the factors; you do not add up the percentages.

items.stem: By what percentage did the number of Deep tech hardware deals increase between 2023 and 2025?

explanation.trap: Using the 2024-2025 period (54 / 45 = +20%) or 2023-2024 (+25%); dividing by 54 gives 33.3%; 18.0% mistakes the absolute increase for a percentage.
explanation.rule: Check the years asked for in the stem before reading the chart.

items.stem: What percentage of the total value of 2025 deals came from Semiconductors (to the nearest 0.1%)?

steps: 2025 value (EUR m) = number of deals × average value: Semiconductors 63 × 180 = 11,340; Software 231 × 95 = 21,945; IT services 98 × 60 = 5,880; Deep tech 54 × 75 = 4,050.
explanation.shortcut: Software is worth about twice as much as Semiconductors, and the other two together almost as much as Semiconductors: the share must be around a quarter.
explanation.trap: Using the number of deals (63 / 446 = 14.1%) or the average values alone (180 / 410 = 43.9%); 51.7% is the Semiconductors / Software ratio; 73.8% is the share of the other sectors.
explanation.rule: Value share = Σ(volume × price) of the part / Σ(volume × price) of the total.

items.stem: Assume the number of Software deals grows in 2026 at the same percentage rate as between 2024 and 2025, while the average Software deal value falls by 10%. What would the total value of Software deals be in 2026 (to the nearest EUR 10m)?

explanation.shortcut: 231 / 189 = 11 / 9; multiplied by 0.9 it gives exactly 1.1. Just calculate 21,945 × 1.1.
explanation.trap: Adding the changes (+22.2% - 10% = +12.2%, hence 24,630) instead of multiplying them; ignoring the fall in average value (26,820); using the 2023-2024 growth (-10%) leads to 17,780.
explanation.rule: Value = volume × price: growth factors multiply, (1 + g1) × (1 + g2) - 1.

items.stem: What were total annual sales of the Supermarket format in 2025?

steps: Total Supermarket floor space: 120 stores × 1,500 m2 = 180,000 m2.
explanation.trap: Forgetting the number of stores (1,500 × 9,000 = 13.5m) or getting the EUR 000 conversion wrong (162m); 900m and 1,040m are Convenience and Hypermarket.
explanation.rule: Write down the unit of each column and convert only once, at the end.

items.stem: What share of the chain's total sales area is accounted for by Convenience stores (to the nearest 0.1%)?

steps: Floor space by format (m2): Hypermarket 20 × 8,000 = 160,000; Supermarket 120 × 1,500 = 180,000; Discount 80 × 1,000 = 80,000; Convenience 300 × 250 = 75,000.
explanation.shortcut: 75 / 495 is a little more than 75 / 500 = 15%: so 15.2%.
explanation.trap: Using the number of stores (300 / 520 = 57.7%) or the share of sales (900 / 4,400 = 20.5%); dividing by the floor space of the other formats gives 17.9%; 25.0% is one format out of four.
explanation.rule: Use the same measure (floor space, stores, sales) in the numerator and the denominator.

items.stem: Which format generates the highest operating profit per m2 of sales area?

steps: Operating profit per m2 = sales per m2 × operating margin.
Hypermarket 6.5 × 3.0% = 0.195; Supermarket 9.0 × 4.5% = 0.405; Discount 10.5 × 5.0% = 0.525; Convenience 12.0 × 6.0% = 0.720 (EUR 000 per m2).
The highest is Convenience (EUR 720 per m2).
explanation.shortcut: Convenience has both the highest sales per m2 and the highest margin: it wins without any calculation.
explanation.trap: Choosing Supermarket because it has the highest total operating profit (EUR 72.9m) or Hypermarket because it has the largest stores.
explanation.rule: If one option dominates on every factor of a product, it is the answer: just check that no other factors are missing.

items.stem: What was the total annual interest cost of savings accounts and term deposits combined?

steps: Balances: savings 25% × 36.0bn = EUR 9.0bn; term deposits 18% × 36.0bn = EUR 6.48bn.
explanation.trap: Applying the simple average rate (2.4%) to the sum of the balances gives 371.5m; 467.6m is the cost of all deposits; 1,728m applies 1.8% + 3.0% to the total; 3,564m is a scale error.
explanation.rule: Interest cost = balance × rate, line by line.

items.stem: What was Valtera Bank's average cost of customer deposits (to the nearest 0.01%)?

steps: Weighted average of the rates, using the shares: 45% × 0.1 + 25% × 1.8 + 18% × 3.0 + 12% × 2.2.
explanation.shortcut: You do not need the total in euros: the shares in the chart are already the weights.
explanation.trap: The simple average of the rates (7.1 / 4 = 1.78%) ignores that current accounts, which are almost free, make up 45%. Excluding current accounts gives 2.28% (weighted average) or 2.33% (simple average); 2.20% is the corporate rate alone.
explanation.rule: Average cost of funding = Σ(share × rate).

items.stem: The bank wants to cut its average cost of deposits to 1.10% by moving money from term deposits into current accounts, keeping total deposits unchanged. How much would need to move (to the nearest EUR 0.1bn)?

steps: Every euro moved from term deposits (3.0%) to current accounts (0.1%) saves 2.9%.
Amount to move: 71.6m / 2.9% = EUR 2.47bn, i.e. EUR 2.5bn.
explanation.shortcut: The average cost must fall by 0.199 points; each point of share moved is worth 0.029 points: you need 0.199 / 0.029 = 6.86% of deposits, i.e. 0.0686 × 36 = 2.47bn.
explanation.trap: Dividing by 3.0% instead of by the rate difference (3.0% - 0.1% = 2.9%) gives 2.4bn; moving from savings (a 1.7% saving) would require 4.2bn. Applying 6.86% to the stock of term deposits instead of the total (6.48 × 6.86% = 0.4bn) uses the wrong base; 6.5bn is the entire stock of term deposits.
explanation.rule: Effect of a mix shift = amount moved × difference between the two rates.

items.stem: Which company has the largest market capitalisation?

steps: Market cap = price × shares: Arvelle 42.0 × 150 = 6,300; Brontec 18.5 × 400 = 7,400.
explanation.shortcut: Quick estimate: 42 × 150 ≈ 6.3bn, 18.5 × 400 ≈ 7.4bn; the other two are below 5bn.
explanation.trap: Choosing Cedris because it has the highest share price: price alone says nothing about size.
explanation.rule: Market capitalisation = share price × number of shares.

items.stem: What is Dunmore Wafer's EV/EBITDA multiple?

explanation.shortcut: Calculate EV before dividing: 6,000 / 750 = 8.
explanation.trap: Using market cap (4,800 / 750 = 6.4x) forgets the debt; subtracting net debt gives 4.8x; adding it twice gives 9.6x; 1.6x is leverage (net debt / EBITDA).
explanation.rule: EV/EBITDA uses enterprise value, which includes net debt, because EBITDA accrues to both shareholders and creditors.

items.stem: Using the median EV/EBITDA multiple of Arvelle Systems, Brontec and Cedris Photonics, what implied share price would you derive for Dunmore Wafer (to the nearest EUR 0.01)?

explanation.trap: Not subtracting net debt (5,500 / 500 = 11.00), adding it instead of subtracting it (13.40), or using the mean multiple (7.59x, which gives 8.99) instead of the median; 9.60 is the current price.
explanation.rule: From multiple to price: EV = multiple × EBITDA; equity = EV - net debt; price = equity / shares.

items.stem: By what percentage did Data centre revenue grow from 2024 to 2025?

explanation.trap: Dividing by 912 gives 37.5%; 50.0% is the 2023-2024 growth; 140% is the 2023-2025 growth; 34.2% mistakes the absolute increase (342) for a percentage.
explanation.rule: % growth = increase / value in the starting year.

items.stem: Which end market's share of total revenue fell by the most percentage points between 2024 and 2025?

steps: 2024 and 2025 shares: Automotive 36.0% and 30.9% (-5.1 points); Industrial 22.4% and 21.0% (-1.4); Consumer 18.8% and 15.6% (-3.2); Data centre 22.8% and 32.6% (+9.8).
The largest fall in points is Automotive.
explanation.shortcut: Automotive starts from the highest share and its revenue falls while the total rises by 12%: it loses share on a large base.
explanation.trap: Choosing Consumer because it has the steepest percentage fall in revenue (-7.2%): the question asks for points of share, not the change in revenue.
explanation.rule: Change in share in points = new share - old share; it depends both on the item's growth and on the total's growth.

items.stem: If Data centre revenue grows by 25% in 2026 and all other end markets stay at their 2025 levels, what share of 2026 revenue will Data centre represent (to the nearest 0.1%)?

explanation.shortcut: Add only the increase (228) to the total: 1,140 / 3,028 ≈ 0.376.
explanation.trap: Dividing by the 2025 total (1,140 / 2,800 = 40.7%) forgets that the total grows; 32.6% is the 2025 share; adding 25 points to the share gives 57.6%; 45.6% uses the 2024 total.
explanation.rule: When a component grows, the total grows too: update the denominator.

items.stem: By what percentage did the total number of subscribers grow from Q1 to Q4 2025 (to the nearest 0.1%)?

explanation.shortcut: 60 / 740 is a little more than 60 / 750 = 8%: so 8.1%.
explanation.trap: Dividing by 800 gives 7.5%; 36.0% and 55.6% are the growth rates of Standard and Premium; 20.0% is Basic's fall.
explanation.rule: For the growth of the total, first add up the series in each period.

items.stem: Based on Q4 2025 subscriber numbers, what percentage of monthly subscription revenue came from Premium subscribers (to the nearest 0.1%)?

steps: Q4 monthly revenue (EUR 000): Basic 320 × 6 = 1,920; Standard 340 × 11 = 3,740; Premium 140 × 18 = 2,520.
explanation.shortcut: Premium is 17.5% of subscribers but pays 18 against an average price of about 10.2 (8,180 / 800): 17.5% × 1.76 ≈ 30.8%.
explanation.trap: Using the share of subscribers (140 / 800 = 17.5%) ignores prices; 51.4% is the Premium price as a share of the sum of the prices (18 / 35); 45.7% is Standard.
explanation.rule: Revenue share = (volume × price) of the item / Σ(volume × price).

items.stem: Assume that after Q4 2025 each plan's subscriber numbers keep changing every quarter by the same absolute amount as between Q3 and Q4 2025, with prices unchanged. In which quarter will monthly revenue, based on end-of-quarter subscribers, first exceed EUR 10.0m?

steps: Effect on monthly revenue per quarter: -30 × 6 + 30 × 11 + 25 × 18 = -180 + 330 + 450 = +600 (EUR 000).
The first time above 10,000 is Q4 2026.
explanation.shortcut: The gap is 10,000 - 8,180 = 1,820 at +600 per quarter: 1,820 / 600 = 3.03, so 4 quarters are needed.
explanation.trap: Stopping at Q3 2026 by rounding 9,980 to 10.0m: the threshold must be exceeded, not just approached.
explanation.rule: With constant increments: periods needed = gap / increment, rounded up.

items.stem: Comparing Florence and Milan, which hotel has the lower RevPAR, and by how much?

explanation.shortcut: Two simple multiplications: 0.75 × 180 = 135; 0.7 × 200 = 140.
explanation.trap: Looking only at ADR (Florence lower by 20) or only at occupancy (Milan lower): RevPAR combines both.
explanation.rule: RevPAR = occupancy × ADR = room revenue / available rooms.

items.stem: What percentage of the group's total 2025 room revenue came from Amalfi (to the nearest 0.1%)?

steps: Room revenue = rooms × days × occupancy × ADR.
explanation.shortcut: Use RevPAR × rooms × days: for the three year-round hotels 365 × (200 × 120 + 135 × 150 + 140 × 200) = 365 × 72,250 = 26.37m; Amalfi 360 × 60 × 200 = 4.32m.
explanation.trap: Forgetting the seasonal opening (365 days for Amalfi as well) gives 23.0%; using the share of rooms gives 11.3%; the share of RevPAR (360 / 835) gives 43.1%.
explanation.rule: Read the notes: different opening periods change the available capacity.

items.stem: Marea plans to add 40 rooms to the Milan hotel. Occupancy for the enlarged hotel is expected to fall to 65%, with ADR unchanged. By how much would Milan's annual room revenue change?

explanation.trap: Counting only the new rooms (40 × 365 × 0.65 × 200 = 1.90m) or keeping occupancy at 70% (2.04m) ignores the fall on the 200 existing rooms; -0.73m considers only that fall; 11.39m is the new total.
explanation.rule: To measure the impact of an expansion, compare the new total with the old total, not just the added part.

items.stem: By what percentage did Renewables generation increase from 2023 to 2025 (to the nearest 0.1%)?

explanation.shortcut: 41 / 95 is a bit more than 41 / 100 = 41%: about 43%.
explanation.trap: Dividing by 136 gives 30.1%; using a single year (2023-2024: 17.9%; 2024-2025: 21.4%); writing the increase in TWh as a percentage (41.0%).
explanation.rule: Multi-year growth = final value / starting value - 1, not the sum of the annual growth rates.

items.stem: What was the average CO2 intensity of total electricity generation in 2025, in Mt of CO2 per TWh (to 3 decimal places)?

steps: 2025 emissions: gas 96 × 0.40 = 38.4 Mt; coal 14 × 0.90 = 12.6 Mt; total 51.0 Mt.
explanation.shortcut: Renewables and nuclear emit zero but count in the denominator. 51 / 306 would be exactly 1/6 (0.1667); with 304 the result is slightly higher: 0.168.
explanation.trap: Dividing only by fossil generation (51 / 110 = 0.464) or taking the simple average of the factors (0.325 across four sources, 0.650 across two); 0.235 is the 2023 intensity.
explanation.rule: Average intensity = total emissions / total output, including zero-emission sources.

items.stem: By what percentage did total CO2 emissions from electricity generation fall between 2023 and 2025 (to the nearest 0.1%)?

explanation.shortcut: Coal emits more than twice as much as gas per TWh and falls sharply: the fall in emissions must be steeper than the fall in fossil generation (24.1%).
explanation.trap: Using fossil generation (from 145 to 110 TWh, -24.1%) ignores the different emission factors; dividing by 2025 gives 38.2%; 18.9% is 2024-2025 only; 44.0% is the fall in coal alone.
explanation.rule: When the components have different weights, calculate the weighted measure in each year and then the change.
